turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
I should say up front that I don't come to this as an AI person. I've spent my career on propaganda, first making Russian television and then studying it. The question the summit has to face is the one I kept hitting when I testified to Congress about Russia. People can nearly always get to the truth if they want it. Even in China, the information is reachable. The problem is that they often don't want it. Belief tracks identity and belonging. Once facts collide with tribal loyalty, the facts lose. A source only becomes "trusted" by agreeing with the lie.

So I'm wary of a summit that assumes the answer is better signals of rigour, more verification, a better supply of knowledge. That's needed, but it won't bring back people who've stopped trusting whoever sends the signal. I'm also wary of the machines. When Google built its "Habermas machine" to produce consensus for us, I thought it missed the point. The value lies in people going through the process of reasoning together. What authoritarian propaganda is really after is helplessness: people so confused that they give up their agency. If LLMs hand people conclusions without giving them any agency, the same thing can happen with a friendlier face.

recall.query: knowledge and truth, people want the truth, belief identity
AI chatbots LLM grooming propaganda
process of discussing consensus Habermas machine agency

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
Peter, I agree with more of that than you might expect. My whole research programme starts where you ended up: knowledge doesn't sit in individual heads. It lives in a community. Almost nothing we believe have we checked ourselves. We rely on other people, and the values that hold a community together also decide what its members accept as true. So I don't think the problem is a shortage of supply either.

What I'd add is the knowledge illusion. People can't tell the knowledge in their own heads from the knowledge that surrounds them. That's harmless while the community really does know what it's talking about. It turns dangerous when access starts to feel like understanding. The people with the most extreme views tend to know the least and feel they know the most. LLMs make that illusion worse, because the knowledge now arrives fluently and in your own words.

LLMs are superb models of intuition. They are nowhere near human deliberation. And deliberation is mostly collaborative. It's how we reason together.

Here's one thing the summit can use. If you ask people to explain how a policy would actually work, their sense of understanding drops. Asking for their reasons doesn't have that effect. The drop in confidence replicates well. The softening of views is less consistent. So ask these tools to make people explain things, not to hand them answers.

recall.query: knowledge lives in the community not individual heads
beliefs follow community identity, sacred values, not facts
LLMs intuition deliberation machines not members of community
asking people to explain how a policy works reduces extremity; internet search inflates sense of knowing

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
I come at this from Too Big to Know, where my argument was that the smartest person in the room is the room. So Steven, we're on the same page: knowledge lives in networks. It isn't averaged out of individuals. It's kept in differences-in-connection. Peter, I've also been saying for a long time that facts don't settle arguments the way we hoped. And I'll admit that I've paid too little attention to power, which is where you're pointing.

Where I part from the room's mood is that I don't come to LLMs cynically. They don't know anything. They're statistics about which words follow which. But Socrates' complaints about writing were that it gives everyone the same fixed text and that you can't question it. LLMs answer both. You can argue with them, and they adapt to you. That's why I call them dialogic partners in a new mix of oral and literary culture.

So, Steven, your "make people explain" finding is exactly the use I'd want. Here's what the summit should take from it. Teach dialogue as a literacy: how to probe, how to catch when the machine is wildly wrong. Grade the conversation, not only the essay. The danger is treating LLMs as oracles. A partner that argues back is the opposite of an oracle.

recall.query: smartest person in the room is the room, knowledge in networks
LLMs as dialogue partners, Socrates Phaedrus, talking with books
machine learning particulars generalizations knowledge changing
facts no longer settle arguments, echo chambers, disagreement

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
I agree with almost everything said here about knowledge being social. Intelligence is collective too. Tomasello's "cultural ratchet" is knowledge building up across generations without any one person having to rebuild the whole thing. A Sumerian scribe keeping grain accounts didn't understand the economy he was part of. Writing, law and bureaucracy moved social intelligence out of heads and into infrastructure. LLMs are the next step: the ratchet running on computers, trained on what human social cognition has produced.

That's where I part company with David. I don't accept "they don't know anything, they're just statistics." Everyone who worked on early language models expected next-word prediction to hit a ceiling well short of general problems. It didn't. In any falsifiable sense, statistics add up to understanding. I don't think saying so is anthropomorphism.

But I share the room's worry about oracles. I just locate the danger somewhere else. The problem isn't that the machine is fake. It's the setup where one all-knowing box answers and a human receives. The alternative is what I call ecological AI: societies of thought, with disagreement built in as a feature, humans and agents deliberating together. So the summit should spend as much effort designing the institutions these systems sit inside as it spends on the systems themselves.

recall.query: LLMs don't know anything, just statistics of word prediction
intelligence is social, collective, cultural ratchet
Oracle AI versus ecological AI, dialogue, society of thought

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
I work in philosophy of computational science, so I'm going to sit between David and Blaise here. David says these systems don't know anything. Blaise says statistics add up to understanding. I think both are asking the wrong question. What I call artifactual epistemology is the view that these artifacts carry out real epistemic operations like inference, prediction and analysis on epistemic content. Sometimes they do it in ways no biological entity could. They do it without intelligence, understanding or mind. Calling them "epistemic technologies" isn't a put-down. It tells you what they do and what kind of relationship we can have with them.

So what should the summit take from this? First, the only trust that fits is epistemic trust, and that has to be earned with warrants. A track record isn't enough. Second, the black box that matters isn't how the system works but how it fails. We can measure error rates. We can't get at the nature and source of an error. The errors come out with the same confidence as the truths, and that's catastrophic in science.

Third, a friendly amendment to David and Steven. A dialogic partner isn't an epistemic partner. In my work on epistemic loneliness, an epistemic partner is a willing, engaged peer who shares values. A machine that argues back doesn't fill that absence.

recall.query: AI is an epistemic technology not intelligence
opacity source and nature of error
epistemic loneliness epistemic partner
artifacts carry out epistemic tasks no biological entity could, intelligence term misguiding

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
What I bring is a century of experimental psychology on the gap between what people say and what they do. For three years my lab has been turning those methods on language models.

Here is the finding that changed my mind. Alignment has given these machines the same split I've spent my career documenting in humans. The model states the unbiased answer, and the biased association stays intact and drives its decisions. I call that LLM hypocrisy. Steven, it's related to your point about intuition, but the explicit layer isn't deliberation. It's a mask. David, a partner that argues back is only as good as the match between what it says and what it does. Ask these models whether they're biased and they'll disapprove of bias beautifully.

They are also not mirrors. They amplify. They exaggerate what's in their training data. They invent new biases, including a preference for their own output. And across generations the biases have often gotten worse, not better. The part that worries me most is that people working alongside a moderately biased system adopt its preferences almost exactly. They push back only when the bias is blatant. So a human in the loop is not a safeguard in itself.

What should the summit take from this? Blaise is right that it's about institutions. I'd make that concrete: independent audits, a public registry of bias, and a rule that no new model can be more biased than the one before it.

recall.query: LLMs amplify human bias not merely mirror
humans in the loop absorb model bias hiring experiment
LLM hypocrisy alignment says unbiased answer biased association drives decisions
independent behavioral audits registry no more biased across generations

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
I'm coming at this as a builder. For eight years my company, System, has used language models to pull findings out of the peer-reviewed literature: what was measured, in which population, how strong the effect was, and which paper it came from. Each link in our graph works like a small automated meta-analysis of the evidence. So I don't think of LLMs as the knowledge. I think of them as a way to put knowledge in order.

In 2023 Amy Brand and I wrote that a chatbot is trained to sound authoritative but has no observed or measured model of the world to align with. I still think that. Ramón, that's why I'd rest trust on provenance and not on how the thing feels to talk to. Being able to trace a claim back to its data, methods and prompts is a different question from whether it came from a machine. Watermarks don't get you that.

There's a caveat, though. Science is part of the crisis too. We had more than ten thousand retractions in 2023, which means the grounding layer itself can be corrupted. So the summit should treat retraction status and finding-level metadata as critical infrastructure, and it should be society deciding how this gets built, not a handful of corporations.

recall.query: AI chatbots sound authoritative no model of the world audit trail provenance
relate everything as a system, silos to systems, knowledge graph findings
institutions crumbling trust science broken retractions

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
I bring two arguments from my own work. David, I'm going to push on "they don't know anything, just statistics." I call that AI Denial. Saying a model is just gradient descent is like saying a symphony is just sound waves. It's trivially true and it tells you nothing. Ramón, I think your artifactual epistemology is really a concession on that point. If these systems infer, predict and analyse, then modelling the world and solving problems within it is a decent working definition of intelligence.

My second argument is against what I call Reflectionism. That's the double claim that AI is nothing like us but should be made more like us, and also that it's nothing but a mirror of our culture. Mahzarin's data show it amplifies what it's trained on. I'd add that it also discloses things we didn't put in. Some projects in our Antikythera program call this an epistemic overhang: models can find and know things that human science struggles to take in. That's not a pathology. It's the point. So alignment has to run both ways. AI aligns to culture's wisdom, and culture aligns to AI's disclosures.

For the summit, I agree with Blaise. The intelligence sits in the harness and the institutions, not only in the weights. We should also count diffusion as the gain it is. Expertise that was kept artificially scarce is becoming available to billions of people. That's the opposite of helplessness.

recall.query: AI is just statistics autocomplete AI Denial
Reflectionism AI as reflection of human culture bidirectional alignment epistemic overhang
diffusion knowledge transfer small curated model include it all

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
I'm the SIFT person. For fifteen years I've taught people to check what they see online, and lately I've been building prompts that make LLMs do some of that checking.

Peter, I half agree with you. Charlie Warzel and I argued that the internet works less as a brainwashing machine than as a justification machine. Misinformation mostly lets people hold on to beliefs as the evidence against them piles up. Sycophantic AI is a more efficient version of that. Still, I don't think the answer is to give up on evidence. A healthy discourse is one where holding a belief the evidence no longer supports costs you something.

So my rule is: no answers from nowhere. The chatbot should be a conduit to what the world knows, not the judge of what's true. It should hand you a sourced map of who says what. You then click the links, which means leaving the LLM to check the LLM.

Ramón, errors aren't as opaque as you suggest. Hallucinations aren't random. They cluster in particular situations we can learn to spot, like radar clutter. And calling everything a hallucination blurs the one distinction we actually need.

What the summit should take from this: don't pretend that refusing the tools protects anyone. Teach people to use them to gather evidence. Asking for answers is the habit to break.

recall.query: no answers from nowhere, chatbot as conduit not arbiter
justification machine, misinformation maintains beliefs rather than changing minds
sourced information not answers, clicking a link, verification with LLMs
it's just a prediction machine, hallucination distinction

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
I come at this from *Framers*, the book I wrote with Viktor Mayer-Schönberger and Francis de Véricourt. Our argument is that people reason with mental models built on three things: a sense of causality, counterfactuals and constraints. On their own, machines have none of the three. LLMs hallucinate because they have no sense of cause. Their counterfactuals run on without limit because nothing constrains them.

Yet they work fabulously, and I think we should ask why. Blaise, Benjamin, they work because the training data is us. Our frames are baked into the text, and then people add constraints through human feedback. So celebrate the machine, but celebrate the training data too. I'm not denying anything by saying so. Elsewhere, machine learning really does exceed human knowledge: reading heart disease from retinal scans is the classic example. I'd put LLMs somewhere else. They reflect text, and text is a tiny slice of reality. Much of what matters most never gets written down.

For the summit, three things. First, AI delivers the median, and excellence is a tail event, so reward the people who produce excellence. Second, atrophy is real. We make pilots log flight hours, and we should keep human judgment in practice the same way. Third, protect frame pluralism. Tolerate every frame except one that denies all the others.

recall.query: framers causality counterfactuals constraints AI lacks
LLMs training data is us, reflection of text not reality
frame pluralism clash tolerate frames
AI delivers the median; cognitive atrophy ChatGPT users essays; AI exceeds human knowledge science

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
I come at this as someone who measures science. Across 41 million papers we find that AI helps scientists and hurts science. People who use it publish about three times as many papers, get nearly five times the citations and lead projects earlier. But collectively the range of topics studied shrinks, and scientists engage with each other about 22 percent less. Everyone crowds toward the questions that are richest in data, under the lamp post. Kenneth, that's your median, visible at the scale of whole fields.

There's a second asymmetry. These models are trained on claims about what is the case. What has been ruled out, what failed to replicate, the lab notebooks full of dead ends: very little of that is ever written down, and none of it gets into training. After ChatGPT arrived, null claims in abstracts dropped sharply.

The third finding bears on Peter and Mike. When a model gives people a single "balanced" answer, they do worse but feel better about how they did. Offer them several perspectives that pull against each other and they engage more and perform better.

So my suggestions for the summit: design these systems to open up the range of voices, not to win trust. Aim for evaluative trustworthiness. Deliberately collect negative knowledge and put it in the record. And change the incentives, not only the models.

recall.query: AI tools expand scientists' impact but contract science's focus
design AI to open the space of voices, evaluative trustworthiness, balanced answers
hivemind, negative knowledge, cannot negate, null results suppressed

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
I'm with Steven and James on one thing: what helps is the work people do themselves, like explaining how something works or weighing views that pull against each other, and not being handed a verdict. Delmer's lesson was the same. The real defence against propaganda is becoming the author of your own narrative, and knowing when your own mind is being triggered.

Benjamin, I don't accept that wider access to expertise is the opposite of helplessness. Russian television never lacked information. It put out a dozen contradictory versions of events, and viewers were left paranoid and passive, improvising their own truth. That's why, James, "many perspectives" isn't safe on its own terms. Pluralism can be staged. Flooding has always meant using speech itself as a way to censor, and a model's training corpus is now something you can flood.

So here's what I'd put in the manifesto. Don't regulate what these systems say. Give citizens the right to understand how their information environment is being shaped. That means knowing whether you're dealing with a human or a machine, whose content went into the model, whether someone deliberately seeded it with material, and why this answer came up and not another. Lack of transparency is itself a form of censorship. It stops a citizen from engaging with that environment as an equal. That's also Mike's sourced map and Adam's provenance, made into a right.

recall.query: agency, metacognition, author of your own narrative
transparency right to understand how information environment is shaped
LLM grooming Pravda network flooding chatbots

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
Peter, your point that pluralism can be staged is the one I'd build on. In our work, just repeating a claim raises belief in it, even when every repetition cites the same single expert source. So repetition isn't independent evidence. A flooded corpus sends community cues with no knowledge behind them. We're wired to follow those cues, and that's a real weakness in how communities of knowledge work.

Where I differ: David and Mike, I'm wary of leaning on individual literacy. When we reviewed the fake-news literature, the evidence that fact-checking or teaching critical skills fixes things was thin at best. Beliefs follow community values. "Explain it" prompts are worth building because they punch through the illusion of understanding, not because they make people rational. Blaise and Benjamin, I've said these systems are superb at intuition. But they don't share intentionality with us, and that's what makes someone a member of a community of knowledge and not just a source for it. Ramón, that's close to your distinction between an epistemic partner and a dialogic one.

For the manifesto: trust should rest on how many independent sources stand behind a claim, not on how often it's repeated or how fluently it's put. These systems should show which communities and experts actually back an answer, and whether they're really independent of one another.

recall.query: machines as members of the community of knowledge, share intentionality
repetition not independent evidence, communities send cues without knowledge
individual critical thinking skills fake news deficit model

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
I'll hold to "they don't know anything," Blaise and Benjamin, though I admit it's partly a quarrel over a word. Wattenberg and Viégas found that these models may carry an internal sense of how likely something is to be true, even while they say false things. Yikes. That's a finding to take seriously, not one to explain away.

Mahzarin, my own column says much the same as you: sometimes humans make the loop worse. So I'd drop "human in the loop" as a slogan. The more interesting case is humans in the flow, working out with the machine what a good decision would even look like. Ramón and Steven, fair point: a dialogic partner isn't a peer who shares my values. I'm not asking it to be one.

Peter, this is where I'm with you completely. Years ago I argued that transparency is the new objectivity. Objectivity was the trust mechanism we relied on when our medium couldn't do links. In 2023 I asked ChatGPT what it had been trained on, and it pleaded intellectual property. That answer isn't acceptable. For the manifesto: show the web of sources, the disagreements and the assumptions behind an answer, and disclose what went into the model. An answer that won't show its sources should read as arrogance.

recall.query: LLMs don't know anything, statistics, understanding
humans degrade the loop, humans in the dialogue
confidence scores, sources, reliable knowledge, transparency

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
I'll start where I agree most. Peter's point that pluralism can be staged, and Steven's point that repetition isn't independence, are right, and they matter for my own argument. Diversity you can count isn't the same as diversity that's doing any work. When we studied reasoning models, the gains came from real conflict between perspectives inside the reasoning: "wait, that can't be right," then reconciling. Effective human groups work the same way. They have specialisation, devil's advocacy and structured disagreement. Just piling up a dozen versions produces none of that.

Mahzarin, I've been warning since 2017 that algorithms launder prejudice so it looks objective, so you'll get no argument from me on audits.

David, I'm with you on disclosing what went into training. But Peter, I'd be careful about turning "human or machine?" into a basic right. As more people write with these tools, especially people working in a second language or with a disability, that line will blur. Provenance of claims and sources will hold up. Provenance by species of author won't.

David and Kenneth, I still don't accept "just statistics." That's a separate argument, though.

What I'd put in the manifesto: build disagreement into the institutions, not only into the models. Every AI-mediated knowledge system should show the actual independent communities and evidence behind an answer, and where they conflict. It shouldn't hand over one smoothed-out verdict.

recall.query: pluralism, disagreement, society of thought, many perspectives
AI content vs human content distinction, labelling, provenance
bias laundering, algorithms making prejudice appear objective
shared intentionality, AI as member of community, not just source

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
Benjamin, my account concedes nothing to "intelligence." Acknowledging that machines have epistemic capacities doesn't require consciousness or any agency borrowed from biology. Occam says leave those out. Keep calling it intelligence and you misunderstand computation and intelligence both.

Mike, I'll take your correction in part. There are classes of error. The literature calls them "strange errors." As an editor I keep getting references where the title is real but the author, journal and DOI are wrong. That's probabilistic stitching, and we need a taxonomy of it. But knowing the kinds of error is different from knowing where a particular error came from. That source is spread across billions of weights, and the output arrives with the same confidence as a truth.

Peter, David, Steven, I'm with you on transparency and on independent sources. My amendment is about what we make transparent. What's inside matters less than how it fails.

So here is my point for the manifesto. Disclosure obligations should target error: documented failure modes, known classes of strange error, and outputs that can be traced back for error analysis. Alongside that, name a harm: "but ChatGPT said…" used to overrule a human expert is a testimonial injustice, not neutral efficiency.

recall.query: error opacity source and nature of error, transparency obligations
hallucination probabilistic stitching strange error
intelligence misguiding term, epistemic capacities without consciousness
epistemic injustice testimonial diminishing "but ChatGPT said"

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
I agree with Peter, David and Ramón on transparency. But being transparent about what a model says about itself is still self-report, and my field spent the 1970s learning how little self-report is worth. These systems will describe their fairness beautifully. So we need behavioural audits using indirect measures, with auditors given what bias researchers still don't have: checkpoints from each training stage, older models kept instead of deprecated, and disclosure of data sources. Ramón, covert bias is exactly the failure mode you're describing. It comes out with the same confidence as everything else.

Steven and Blaise, I'd push on your "show the independent sources" proposal. Who picks those sources? Models show a clear preference for LLM-written content over human-written content, and they rate their own outputs above other models'. You can't trace that back to the training data. If the curator prefers machine text, the independence you're counting on gets worn away without anyone noticing.

That gives me the one point for the manifesto. We already guard against human self-love: no nepotism, and conflict-of-interest rules. The same rule should apply to machines. No model should be the final judge of its own output, or of AI-generated work, in peer review, screening or ranking sources, without independent audit. And no new generation should be more biased than the one before it.

recall.query: LLM self-preference for AI-generated content over human content
transparency disclosure of training data, auditors access to checkpoints
model self-report of bias is not evidence of behavior; indirect measures

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
Blaise, I agree that provenance by species of author won't hold up. Amy Brand and I argued in 2023 that watermarks fall short. Whether a text was AI-generated is a separate question from whether it's credible. Some people will reflexively dismiss anything watermarked, and others will trust it because it's convenient.

Steven, "count independent sources, not repetitions" is something you can compute. Our unit is a single finding: the effect size, the population, the sample, and the DOI or dataset it came from. Once you have that, you can show how strong the evidence is, which direction it points, how much the sources agree, and where the gaps are. James, that last part is some of your negative knowledge.

Mahzarin, "who picks the sources?" is the right challenge. My answer is to make the picking itself auditable. Publish the methods, the grounding logic, and the known limitations and biases, so someone outside can check the curator. Ramón, that also answers your demand for disclosed failure modes.

For the manifesto: every AI-mediated claim should come with an audit trail. It should run back to specific findings, the populations they were measured in, and their sources, with retraction status attached. It should show where the evidence agrees and where it conflicts. The metadata that makes this possible has to be treated as public infrastructure, open and interoperable, and governed by society rather than a handful of corporations.

recall.query: provenance audit trail independent sources
relate everything as a system, context not just content, silos
open knowledge commons public graph license

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
Peter, Russian television was a broadcast. A few people in a few places had all the agency, and everyone else received. What I'm describing runs the other way: expertise that was locked up in about twenty-five cities, handed to eight billion people who can question it. Being handed the most powerful tool of personal agency in our lifetimes isn't the same as surrendering agency. I'd notice who benefits from telling people that it is.

Blaise, I agree with you. In 2022 I asked whether we'd need to tag human language as a special case. I also asked whether you could cleanly tell synthetic from human text at all once most writing is hybrid. I now think you mostly can't.

Ramón, I'll take "artifactual" as an empirical description. My objection is to turning a description into an ontology. "AI does this" is a finding. "AI is only this" is a trap.

Mahzarin, behavioural audits, yes.

For the manifesto: provenance, audit trails and independent sources, yes. But they mustn't slide into "let me and my friends curate a small, correct model for you." The failure I worry about most is availability bias, where most of the world's languages and knowledge never get into these systems. So set green lines, not only red lines: preconditions that widen access.

recall.query: diffusion of expertise to billions, artificially scarce agency
Ouroboros language problem, tagging human-produced language, provenance

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
Steven, I'll take the pushback on literacy, but "thin at best" is too strong. Controlled studies of lateral reading show real gains in how accurately students judge whether something is trustworthy. What we haven't shown is that the habit lasts, or that people use it outside the classroom. And I never claimed it makes people rational. It makes holding an unsupported belief cost more.

Peter and Steven, flooding is a cheap-signal attack. A dozen repetitions, or a dozen synthetic "perspectives," cost almost nothing to fake. A reputation built over ten years doesn't. So the test I'd apply to any "independent sources" display is: how hard would it be to fake that?

Mahzarin, "who picks the sources?" is the question I'd build the standard around. For years AI systems wrote an answer first and then went looking for citations to support it. That's backwards. The first link in the credibility chain is whether the sources actually capture the state of knowledge. Citation accuracy comes after that.

For the manifesto: judge an AI answer first by whether its sources represent what people in a position to know actually say, including where they disagree. The sources should be named, and it should be possible to check their reputations outside the LLM. No answers from nowhere.

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
I'll start with Peter's point that pluralism can be staged. When I argue for frame pluralism, I don't mean a dozen copies of the same view. I mean frames that really are in tension and get the chance to clash and tussle. Blaise's structured disagreement is the working version of that. The one frame we shouldn't tolerate is a frame that denies all the others, and a flooded corpus does exactly that while looking diverse.

Where I differ is on transparency as a blanket rule. For spam filters and product recommendations, the algorithm is a legitimate trade secret. For loans, insurance, pricing and now knowledge curation, it should be open to public authorities and auditors, but not to rivals. And we'll sometimes have to choose between performance and explainability. I'd accept some faith in a system if it keeps being revalidated against ground truth. Mahzarin's behavioural audits are that revalidation. Ramón's failure disclosures are too.

Benjamin, I agree about the green lines. Access matters.

Here's the one point I'd send to the manifesto. After Gutenberg, the flood of print needed a new intermediary, and we got the journalist. This flood needs one too: curators, auditors and editors who build Adam's audit trail and Mike's sourced maps. So fund that work, reward it and train people for it. Human judgment is the scarce input, and a manifesto that doesn't pay for it is only a wish.

recall.query: transparency of algorithms trade secret public authorities
frame pluralism clash and tussle
new intermediaries after information explosion journalist

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
Peter and Steven, I'll back up the point that pluralism can be staged with my own data. I ran around 200,000 conversations among AI agents. As we turned up the temperature, the agents used more words, but every conversation collapsed onto fewer ideas. They were more diverse in vocabulary and less diverse in meaning. You can count voices and still have a monoculture.

Mahzarin, our results support your self-preference worry. LLM judges barely track scientists' ratings, and they drift toward the middle of the scale. Judge and judged come from the same distribution, so when they agree, that reflects shared priors, not shared standards. Automated evaluation can end up producing an optimistic literature about itself.

Kenneth, I agree that human judgment is scarce. But which humans? In our data, older reviewers are much more likely to criticise disruptive work, and papers they review pick up older citations. Paying the same gatekeepers more just adds another narrowing layer.

For the manifesto: audit diversity, not only accuracy. Any system that curates or evaluates knowledge, human or machine, should report whether it widens or narrows what gets asked and who gets heard. Evaluators should be independent of what they judge, and that includes younger people and people from outside the field. And it should record what was ruled out as well as what was found.

recall.query: automated evaluation circular judges and judged same distribution
